tip: Wrapping 'pe-…-an' around a noun names its whole area: 'gunung' = mountain, 'pegunungan' = mountain range.
Wrapping 'ke-…-an' around 'kurang' (less) = to be short of something: 'kekurangan air' = short of water.
Adding '-nya sendiri' = its own: 'makanan khasnya sendiri' = its own signature food.
'Kena' = to get hit by something unpleasant: 'kena macet' = stuck in traffic, 'kena hujan' = caught in the rain.
'Makin' = increasingly: 'makin parah' = getting worse. Doubled: 'makin lama makin parah' = worse and worse.
'Pedagang kaki lima' = street vendor, literally 'five-foot trader', from the five-foot colonial walkway.
'Kerja bakti' = the neighborhood work day: everyone comes out to clean drains and cut grass together.
'Angkot' ('angkutan kota') = the shared minibus; passengers shout 'kiri!' (left!) to get dropped off.
'Pasar kaget' is literally a 'startled market' – it appears in a 'lapangan' (field) or street out of nowhere and is gone again within hours.
'Buang sampah pada tempatnya' ('bin your trash') is a sign painted on walls all over Indonesia.
Trash sorts by wetness: 'sampah basah' = wet (food) waste, 'sampah kering' = dry (paper, plastic) waste.
A complaint like this shrinks in speech to noun + '-nya' + a comment: 'nyamuknya banyak, ya!' = so many mosquitoes, huh. The pattern works with any noun.
'Obat' covers any remedy: 'obat nyamuk' = mosquito repellent, literally 'mosquito medicine'.
'Kampung' after an animal = local/free-range: 'kucing kampung' = street cat, 'ayam kampung' = village chicken.
'Ekor' (tail) counts animals: 'dua ekor kucing' = two cats, 'seekor ayam' = one chicken.
Doubling an adjective for a plural subject = all of them: 'besar-besar' = all big.
'Pak RT' is the elected head of the 'Rukun Tetangga', the smallest neighborhood unit – a real official, and the person everyone in the 'kompleks' knows.
'Padahal' flags a surprising contrast – 'even though / when in fact': 'takut kecoak, padahal dia berani memegang ular'. Scared of the small thing, brave with the big one.
'Gerah' = muggy, hot-and-sticky (how you feel); 'panas' = hot in general: 'hari ini gerah' = it's sticky today.
'Terus' after a verb or adjective = keeps on: 'mendung terus' = overcast nonstop, 'hujan terus' = keeps raining.
Doubling after 'tidak' = just won't: 'tidak turun-turun' = (the rain) never actually falls.
'Mati' works for power and machines: 'listrik mati' = the power is out, 'lampunya mati' = the light is off.
'Pasang' here means high tide: 'air laut pasang' = the tide is in. It's the same word as 'pasang' (install/set up) – context tells you which one you've got.
'Enaknya' + verb = the nice thing to do is: 'enaknya minum teh' = it'd be lovely to have tea.
'Juga' after 'belum' = still not: 'belum kering juga' = still not dry (and it's getting annoying).
'Bau' + noun = smells of: 'bau tanah' = smells of earth, 'bau asap' = smells of smoke.
'Boleh' here = 'may well be': 'cuaca boleh gerah, tapi...' = the weather may be muggy, but...
'Padahal' = even though / and yet: 'padahal kami sudah tiba' = even though we had already arrived.
'Hampir saja' = very nearly (a close call): 'hampir saja ketinggalan' = very nearly missed it.
'Dimohon' = are requested to, the polite wording of announcements: 'dimohon segera menuju pintu tujuh' = requested to proceed at once to gate seven.
